messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Animals: Dogs, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Priya's Vigil

Priya was sixty-one when she came to the clinic, her appointment card held in hands that trembled slightly as she sat in the waiting room. She had worked the orchards and fields around the Central Valley for nearly forty years, and her body bore the marks of that labor—weathered skin, a permanent stoop in her posture, fingers stiffened by repetitive motion. But it was something else that had brought her here now, something she had carried silently through decades and could no longer manage alone.

The assault had happened in the autumn of 1998, on a late afternoon when she was alone in the storage shed behind the farm where she worked. A man had followed her in—someone she recognized from the neighboring property—and what happened in those minutes had fractured something fundamental in how she understood her own body and the world around it. He had held her down. She remembered his weight, the smell of his sweat and tobacco, the way her voice had seemed to come from someone else entirely when she tried to scream. When he finally left, she had sat in the dust for an hour, unable to move, unable to fully believe what had just occurred.

For the first few years, Priya had tried to continue as though nothing had changed. She returned to work. She did not report the assault—she was undocumented then, afraid of losing her job, afraid of not being believed. She kept the secret even from her husband, Rajesh, though he sensed something had shifted in her. She had begun to flinch when he reached for her in bed. She had stopped letting him hold her from behind.

By her mid-fifties, the symptoms had become impossible to hide. The intrusive memories arrived without warning, with a vividness that obliterated the present moment. A dog barking in a neighbor's yard would trigger the full sensory replay—she would be back in the shed, the memory playing like a film loop, each frame as immediate and terrifying as the original moment. Her body would react before her mind had time to catch up; her heart would race, her breath would shallow, and she would feel the phantom pressure of hands on her wrists. When this happened at work, in the fields or at the packing station, she would have to excuse herself, sometimes spending twenty minutes in the bathroom stall trying to convince herself that she was safe, that it was 2024, not 1998.

Sleep had become a battleground. Priya lay awake most nights, her body rigid beside Rajesh, her attention fixed on the sounds of the house—the creak of the floorboards, the wind against the windows. She could not afford to sleep deeply. Danger, she had come to believe, required constant vigilance. If she let her guard down, something terrible would happen. The irrationality of this belief did not diminish its grip on her.

Intimacy with Rajesh had become nearly impossible. When he touched her unexpectedly—reaching for her hand while she stood at the stove, placing a hand on her shoulder as he passed—she would startle violently, her whole body going rigid with alarm before she could recognize that it was him. The look of hurt in his eyes, repeated over and over across the years, had become its own form of pain. She loved him. She wanted to be the woman he had married. But her body no longer trusted touch, and no amount of conscious reassurance could override the alarm system that had been rewired inside her.

At sixty-one, Priya had finally told Rajesh the truth. She had cried as she spoke, and he had held her—carefully, aware now of how her body responded to his closeness. He had asked why she had never sought help, and she had not known how to answer. There was shame. There was the fear that speaking about it would make it more real. But mostly there was the exhaustion of carrying it alone, the sense that her body had become a hostile place, and the growing terror that she was losing her marriage, her peace, and her self to a man who had taken only minutes but stolen decades.

It was Rajesh who had found the clinic and made the appointment. Priya sat in the waiting room now, afraid of what help might look like, but more afraid of continuing as she was.
